units: a spokeswoman for a neighborhood group lays out their demands
she sorts these demands into three headings
the first heading concerns street lamps that stop working at night
the second heading deals with waste left on the ground
the third heading targets the danger of a crossing that is too narrow
an occupant of a nearby dwelling reports a work site barrier that blocks the view
a public official announces that a study has begun
a meeting open to the public is promised for soon
every household that signed will receive a written reply
text: Speaking for the neighborhood group, the woman at the microphone sorted the complaints under three headings. Lighting came first. Every other lamp along the lane behind the old workshop, she said, goes dark as soon as night falls. Cleanliness came second: cigarette ends piled at the foot of the benches, sacks dumped beside the bins instead of inside them. The crossing came third, where bicycles and delivery vans fight over a roadway too narrow to hold both. A tenant from the corner building spoke up as well. The hoarding around the work site next door, he said, blocks what you can see from the sidewalk. The official handling the file answered that a study is already under way, and that an open meeting will be held before the season ends. Every household that signed the register left out last week will get a written reply.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first communities gathered near a source of water
that place gave rise to the notion of common ground
a well was dug first, then ringed with a low rim
a stone seat there took in the oldest members
shared business was argued out beside the well
as the settlements spread, arcades rose around the open ground
trade came to stand alongside public speech
a roofed building then kept the traders out of bad weather
the place served to announce and to challenge common decisions
text: Long before streets carried names, people came together where the water was, and out of that habit grew the idea of ground belonging to everyone. A well was sunk first. A low rim went up around it, and after the rim a bench of stone, where the oldest of the settlement sat through the afternoon. Whatever touched the whole community came to be argued beside that well. As the settlements spread, arcades rose along the edges of the open ground, and goods began to change hands where only words had. Later a roofed hall was raised, its pillars keeping the stalls dry when storms broke at dusk. The square ended as the place where shared decisions were read out, listened to, and shouted down when they displeased. Out of that slow layering comes the stubborn attachment people still feel for an emptiness ringed by walls.

units: the tiredness caused by noise at night depends above all on the shape of the surrounding walls
hard surfaces send sound back instead of soaking it up
a shout in a closed courtyard returns as an echo to the sleeper
an abrupt change in level breaks deep sleep
the sleeper can wake without keeping any memory of it
exhaustion lowers the capacity to put up with noise
sharper annoyance leads to complaints
designers use absorbent materials and planting
a soft surface takes energy out of the sound wave
text: What wears people down about noise at night has less to do with how loud it is than with the shape of the walls around the bed. Smooth stone and glass throw sound back rather than soaking it up, so a shout let loose in a closed courtyard returns as an echo to the ear of whoever is trying to sleep. Deep sleep breaks at the slightest jump in level, and the sleeper surfaces without ever recalling it, so the night loses its continuity. The effects stack. Tiredness lowers what a person can put up with, worn tolerance turns an ordinary sound into a nuisance, and the nuisance turns into a complaint. Planners answer with porous materials, hedges set along the fences, and paving that damps the roll of wheels. Every soft surface strips energy from the wave, and a weakened wave stops crossing walls.

units: a dispute grows out of a waste bin left open in a shared courtyard
the residents of one building blame the others for leaving sacks on the ground
those others answer that the passage is blocked by bicycles
the written exchanges turn hostile
two households break off all contact
a building employee suggests drawing a sketch of the courtyard together
each participant was to mark their routes and their drop-off spots
the sketch shows that a sealed doorway forced every route through the same point
reopening that doorway and putting up a low fence end the quarrel
text: It began with a complaint about a bin left standing open in the shared courtyard of a housing block. Residents of the north wing accused those in the south wing of setting their sacks down on the ground, and the south wing answered that the north wing filled the passage with bicycles. Voices rose, letters turned curt, and two households stopped speaking altogether. The caretaker then put forward an odd proposal: bring both sides together, not to argue the matter, but to draw the courtyard. Each person was to mark where things got put down and which way they walked. What the drawing showed was a sealed doorway that pushed everyone through one single point. The doorway was opened again, a low fence divided the ground, and the complaint was withdrawn without any formal proceeding.

units: two ways exist to consult the residents of a housing block
the first sets a voting box in the entrance hall for a week
a slip is dropped into every mailbox
the count takes an evening and two witnesses
having witnesses keeps the result from being challenged
the second way uses an open book where each person writes and signs
a private vote keeps opinions to oneself
the open book puts the reasoning on display and shifts positions
the private vote is chosen for questions that set residents against each other
text: There are two ways to take the opinion of everyone living in a housing block, and they do not serve the same purpose. The first is to stand a voting box in the entrance hall for a week, with a slip dropped into every mailbox. Allow a whole evening for the count, and line up two witnesses so that nobody can argue with the outcome afterward. The second swaps the box for an open book, left on a table by the stairs, where each resident writes an opinion and signs it. A closed vote keeps opinions to oneself and suits subjects that raise tempers. An open book puts the reasoning on display, and people do shift their position once they have read it. Take the box when the question splits households, and the book when what is wanted is a shared view of the matter before anything gets decided.

units: a covered market is described through its different phases
the stalls go up very early
the sellers scrap over the empty wooden supports at that hour
the busy stretch pulls the aisles very tight
parents with strollers give up the visit and leave by the back
the evening clear-out is reckoned the hardest
it means packing up the goods that went unsold
the traders help one another out by lending equipment
one of them keeps an eye on the stall of a trader who has stepped away
text: Push through the swinging door of the covered market and the first thing you hear is the clatter of carts. The place runs on three tempos, and the traders will tell you so straight out. First comes the setup, before dawn, when everyone builds a stall and scraps over the empty pallets. Then comes the crush, when the aisles pull in so tight that strollers give up and head back out the rear door. Last comes the teardown at night, the worst of the three, the one nobody wants to talk about, because the crates that went unsold have to be packed away again. Between those three a quieter life slips in. They save one another a parking spot, lend out a scale, watch a neighbor's stall while he goes off to eat. One seller sums it up laughing. We bicker all day, she says, but we never let go of each other.

units: the cleaning crew has the space to itself at sunrise
they gather the leaves that came down in the night
delivery drivers and then office workers arrive after them
those workers cross the place without paying it any attention
a loud procession of cyclists cuts the space in two
the public seats fill up in early afternoon
a water basin has been out of service since the cold season
its rim does duty as a ledge for setting bags down
late in the evening the eating places carry their seats outside
text: At sunrise the plaza belongs to the sweepers, who push the night's fallen leaves ahead of them in long dry heaps. The delivery vans come next, then the office workers, who cut across on the diagonal without once looking up. A column of cyclists splits the open ground down the middle, horns and whistles all mixed together, and vanishes down the lower avenue. By early afternoon the benches have filled: retired men, teenagers perched on the backrests, a mother keeping watch on a stroller. The fountain in the middle has been shut off since the cold set in, and its rim now does duty as a ledge for bags. When the sun drops behind the roofs, the color of the place changes and so does the crowd. The eating places carry their chairs out, windows light up one by one, and the stone still gives back the heat it took in.

units: public seats have been taken away in front of a building
the place now stands empty
that emptiness follows directly from taking the seats away
the removal answered late gatherings and litter
a smell that would not clear was invoked as well
the seats also served people who caused no trouble
an elderly woman used to break her walk there
with nothing to sit on, the usual presence of passersby disappears
the presence of seated people kept the spot safe
text: The benches in front of the building were carried off, and now everyone wonders why nobody stops there anymore. That is no accident. It is a result. Whoever decided to pull them out started from a real grievance: crowds gathering late, empty bottles, a smell that would not clear from under the arcade. Take away the seat and you take away the crowd, and the arithmetic looked sound. But the seat had never served only the people who caused trouble. It served the old woman who breaks her walk in two, the delivery man catching his breath, the boy waiting on a friend. With nothing to sit on, those people no longer stop, and the space empties of its ordinary witnesses. And it was the eyes of seated passersby that kept the forecourt safe. In driving out the use nobody wanted, we drove out the mild watch that held it in check.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a professional practices mediation in a very crowded district
she takes on disputes that the courts will not look into
most complaints concern noise, waste and parking
punishment sharpens tension without changing habits
she starts by listing the complaints building by building
she marks the spots where one household's movements disturb another's rest
she holds short meetings given over to a single question
the commitments people make are written down
a check follows about six weeks later
text: She handles mediation in a densely built district, taking on the disagreements that neither the police nor the courts care to open a file on. The starting problem is one of numbers: most of the conflicts reported turn on noise, on how the waste gets moved around, and on parking, and none of those three yields to punishment, which hardens positions without altering habits. Her method works in steps that can be measured. She lists the complaints building by building, then marks the points where one household's comings and goings run into another household's rest. After that she calls short meetings, each given over to a single question, and writes down what people commit to. A check follows six weeks later. Files that reopen after that check, she says, make up a very small share of her year's work.

units: two makeovers of nearby spaces are set side by side
the first concerns a school yard given a cushioned surface
that spot also holds planters and wooden tiers
the children spread across it unevenly
every fixture imposes one single way of using it
the second job took over an abandoned lot for far less money
it looks unfinished, with rough low walls
a wider range of activity is seen there
the absence of any imposed use accounts for that range
text: Two makeovers a few steps apart invite comparison, and the verdict is not the one the drawings promised. The first gave the school yard a cushioned surface, planters, and wooden tiers to sit on. The work is careful, yet the children spread across it badly, since every fixture assigns one posture and leaves little room for invention. The second went up on abandoned ground nearby, cost a good deal less, and looks unfinished: packed earth, rough low walls, young trees fenced off behind temporary panels. And yet the range of what happens there beats anything the first one manages, for the plain reason that nothing on the site tells you what a surface is meant for. Designers would do well to keep the lesson. The most polished scheme is not always the one that takes in the richest life.
